claim: In the actual read version—the six-page 1991 IEEE Conference on Decision and Control paper by R. Colbaugh, H. Seraji, and K. Glass, not the unread 1993 journal extension—the authors formulate direct adaptive impedance control as three linked components: a Cartesian impedance filter that converts reference motion and measured contact force into a desired end-effector trajectory, a direct adaptive Cartesian controller whose gains are updated without identifying the robot's physical parameters, and a Cartesian-force-to-joint-torque map that can exploit redundancy. Their Lyapunov analysis supports global boundedness and convergence of impedance-tracking errors to a compact residual set under bounded force-sensor error and modeled regularity bounds; the residual can be reduced by gains, while asymptotic tracking is stated only for slowly varying task-space dynamics with negligible force-measurement error. The conference paper provides no presented experiment and no general passivity guarantee.
claim_locator: Actual read version: Proceedings of the 30th IEEE Conference on Decision and Control, Brighton, England, December 1991, pp. 2410–2415
Section 3, Adaptive Cartesian Impedance Control Scheme, equations (8)–(18)
epistemic_status: qualified: controller structure and Lyapunov bounds are directly stated in the 1991 conference text; asymptotic tracking has additional stated conditions, and simulation or experimental effectiveness is not demonstrated within the read paper
problem_and_setting: An n-joint rigid manipulator, possibly kinematically redundant, must realize a user-specified Cartesian mass–damping–stiffness relationship between end-effector position error and environment contact force. The scheme is intended to cover constrained contact and free-space tracking without switching between separate position and force controllers, while avoiding precise robot dynamic parameters and explicit inverse kinematics.
method_or_mechanism: The desired impedance is M(ẍr−ẍ)+B(ẋr−ẋ)+N(xr−x)=P, normally with positive diagonal M, B, and N. A second-order filter driven by reference trajectory xr and measured contact force Pm generates xd, the trajectory whose close tracking realizes that impedance. Defining a weighted Cartesian error q=ė+Ke, the controller computes F=A(t)ẍd*+B(t)[ẍẋ]+f(t)+Pm+Kpe+Kve, where A, B, and f are direct adaptive counterparts of task-space inertia, Coriolis/centripetal, and gravity terms rather than estimates of a physical parameter vector. The final adaptation laws use proportional-plus-integral, e1-modification-like leakage terms driven by error magnitude and task signals. F is mapped to joint torque: T=JᵀF for nonredundant robots; for redundant robots, the underdetermined inverse of a torque-to-Cartesian-force map can use generalized inverses or augmented coordinates to satisfy secondary kinematic objectives.
content_summary: The paper contrasts indirect adaptive control, which estimates a linearly parameterized dynamic model, with direct adaptation of controller gains. Its architecture separates desired impedance specification from robot tracking and redundancy resolution. The filter requires only integration of a simple desired impedance model, especially simple for diagonal gains. The Cartesian controller is designed from a task-space robot model but assumes no detailed structure or parameter values beyond compatible dimensions and regularity bounds used in analysis. A Lyapunov candidate combines tracking errors with adaptive-gain errors. Bounded sensor error and bounded task-space terms yield a derivative inequality in which higher-order negative terms dominate lower-order positive terms, implying convergence to a compact set and global stability; increasing gains can make the residual tracking bound arbitrarily small in the continuous-time analysis. The authors additionally state that if task-space dynamics vary slowly relative to adaptation and force/torque measurement error is negligible, the tracking is asymptotic. Section 4 sketches a physically realizable joint-torque mapping and secondary-task use of redundancy. No numerical results, experimental setup, plots of performance, or contact-task trial are included; only an unshown simulation study is cited as work to appear.
synthesis_role: Represents an early move from model-dependent impedance realization toward online direct adaptation in Cartesian space: it adapts controller coefficients needed to emulate a fixed desired impedance rather than learning the desired impedance itself. It also integrates redundancy resolution into impedance control, but leaves contact passivity, sampled-data effects, quantitative robustness, and experimental validation unresolved.
development_link: Relative to Hogan-style fixed impedance, the advance is adaptive realization under uncertain robot dynamics and a unified filter/controller/mapping architecture for redundant and nonredundant manipulators. Relative to later variable-impedance learning, M, B, and N remain designer prescribed; the adaptive variables compensate robot dynamics rather than discover task-dependent stiffness or damping. Relative to later stability-certified VIC, this analysis does not address energy injection from time-varying desired gains, because the desired impedance is fixed, and it proves bounded-error stability rather than port passivity.

evidence.finding: A simple Cartesian filter maps the specified desired impedance and measured contact force into xd; close tracking of xd is the mechanism for realizing the requested end-effector impedance.

The Cartesian control input uses adaptive matrices A and B and vector f plus measured force and PD terms; the final direct adaptation laws update these controller coefficients without an explicit physical-parameter estimate.
The analysis bounds force-sensor error and task-space model terms, then obtains higher-order negative terms that dominate lower-order positive terms outside a compact set.

The authors state global stability and convergence of tracking errors to a compact residual set, with the residual reducible by gains; they separately state asymptotic stability only when dynamics vary slowly and measurement error is negligible.

The Cartesian input is converted to physical joint torque by JᵀF for nonredundant manipulators; redundant systems admit infinitely many torque solutions and can use generalized-inverse or augmented-coordinate mappings for secondary tasks.
The complete system avoids explicit inverse kinematics and can be reduced to free-space trajectory tracking by removing the impedance filter.
The paper refers to separate computer simulations as indicating good tracking, but presents no simulation figures, numerical tables, or hardware experiment in this six-page version.

boundary_conditions: This card covers only the 1991 IEEE CDC conference version actually read; conclusions or implementation details unique to the unread 1993 Journal of Robotic Systems extension are not transferred.
The desired impedance matrices M, B, and N are specified by the user and are not learned or adapted; the method adapts robot-control coefficients to realize that model.
The main result is global stability with convergence to a compact residual set under bounded disturbances and force/torque sensor error, not exact convergence in the general case.

The claim that the residual can be made arbitrarily small by increasing gains is derived in continuous time; the authors explicitly warn that discretization prohibits excessively large gains and mention moderate sampling near 100 Hz only through an external, unpublished simulation reference.
Asymptotic convergence is stated only when task-space dynamic terms are slowly varying relative to the adaptive elements and force/torque sensor measurement error is negligible.

The controller depends on Cartesian position, velocity-related quantities, desired-trajectory derivatives, measured contact force, and the task-space model structure/bounds used in the derivation even though numerical robot parameters are not required.
The paper does not formulate or prove passivity at the robot–environment port and does not analyze arbitrary active environments, impacts, switching contacts, delays, saturation, or multi-contact.
The F-to-T redundancy treatment is summarized at a high level and points to earlier mapping work; the conference paper does not provide a complete numerical implementation study.
No experiment or self-contained simulation result is presented, so practical robustness and computational claims are not independently supported within this source.
assumptions: The rigid manipulator admits the stated smooth forward kinematics and task-space Lagrangian representation over the operating region.
The desired reference xr is bounded and twice differentiable; the filter solution and required derivatives are bounded.
Desired impedance and feedback matrices have the positive-definite structure used in the derivation, commonly diagonal for simple filter integration.
Force/torque measurement error is bounded for the residual-set result and negligible for the stated asymptotic special case.
Task-space inertia, Coriolis/centripetal, and gravity terms and their derivatives satisfy the bounding relationships used in equations (14)–(17).
Adaptation and feedback gains are positive and chosen so the Lyapunov inequalities hold.
The relevant Jacobian/mapping remains physically realizable; redundancy resolution or augmented coordinates are selected consistently with the primary impedance task.
Continuous-time analysis adequately approximates the implemented sampled controller within the chosen gain and sampling regime.

reported: Indirect adaptive controllers based on explicit parameter estimation can be computationally intensive, require detailed dynamic structure, and may lack robustness to unmodeled dynamics, sensor noise, and disturbances.
The general direct adaptive result leaves a compact residual impedance-tracking error when force-sensor error and other bounded terms are present.
Excessively large gains cannot be used in practical digital implementations because discretization effects may destabilize or invalidate the continuous-time argument.
A quantitative analysis of gain effects on residual error is left for future work.
Applications in remote, harsh, and unstructured environments and fuller exploitation of redundancy are left for future research.
The paper presents no experiment and defers its cited simulation evidence to a separate work to appear.
inferred: Because no passivity or energy-port result is given, global boundedness of the adaptive tracking system should not be read as a universal guarantee of stable contact with every environment.

Although numerical dynamics parameters are unnecessary, the method is not structure-free in an absolute sense: it assumes a rigid-body/task-space form, measurable signals, bounded derivatives, and a valid Cartesian-to-joint mapping.
The use of desired acceleration and differentiated task quantities may amplify noise or create implementation sensitivity, which is not quantified in this paper.
The redundancy mapping can affect secondary performance and feasibility near singularities, but singularity robustness is not analyzed.
The absence of presented quantitative results prevents assessing convergence speed, force regulation accuracy, computational load, or robustness margins.
